items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSION WORK

items.label: text
items.text: In the dot-and-cross diagram for the HO+ ion you can see that the covalent bond that formed between the H2O and the H+ is unusual in that both the shared electrons come from the O. This is called a dative covalent bond or a co-ordinate covalent bond. Once it has been formed, it is exactly the same as a 'normal' covalent bond.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: You have already met the ammonium (NH4⁺) ion, which is obtained when H+ is added to ammonia (NH₃). The hydroxonium ion is the equivalent ion for water. You do not have to remember the name hydroxonium ion.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: To understand the reaction between ammonia and hydrochloric acid in relation to the Arrhenius theory we have to realise that ammonia reacts with water to form OH- ions:

items.label: text
items.text: There is a more general theory of acids and bases that can be used in more situations:

items.label: list_item
items.text: An acid is a proton (hydrogen ion) donor.

items.label: list_item
items.text: A base is a proton (hydrogen ion) acceptor.

items.label: text
items.text: This is called the Bronsted-Lowry theory.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 17.14 A hydrogen ion (H*) is a proton. If an electron is removed from a hydrogen atom, only a proton is left.

items.label: text
items.text: A better way of writing the reaction that occurs when hydrogen chloride dissolves in water is:

items.label: formula
items.text: H _ { 2 } O ( I ) + H C I ( a q ) \rightarrow H _ { 3 } O ^ { + } ( a q ) + C I ^ { - } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: The HCl donates (gives) a proton (H+) to an H2O molecule. So, according to our definition, the HCl is an acid and H2O is a base because it accepts the proton.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 17.15 HCI donates a proton and H20 accepts it.

items.label: text
items.text: The H3O*(aq) ion is called the hydroxonium ion. This is the ion that we usually write simply as H⁺(aq). You can think of it as a hydrogen ion joined to a water molecule. Cl- has a negative charge because the H* left an electron behind when it transferred to the H2O.

items.label: text
items.text: NH3(aq) + H2O(l) = NH4⁺(aq) + OH-(aq) and that hydrochloric acid dissociates to form H+ ions: HCl(aq) → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq) and that the overall reaction involves H+ ions reacting with OH- ions to form water:

items.label: formula
items.text: H ^ { * } ( a q ) + O H ^ { - } ( a q ) \rightarrow H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 17.17 Ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases also react to form ammonium chloride (the white smoke): NH3(g) + HCl(g)= NH4+Cl-(s)

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE REACTION BETWEEN NHAND HCI

items.label: text
items.text: Dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with ammonia solution in a neutralisation reaction to form a salt, ammonium chloride:

items.label: formula
items.text: N H _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H C I ( a q ) \rightarrow N H _ { 4 } C I ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: Ammonium chloride is an ionic salt so we can show the ions that are present:

items.label: formula
items.text: N H _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H C I ( a q ) \rightarrow N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } ( a q ) + C I ^ { - } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: We can see now that, in order to form ammonium chloride, the HCl must donate a proton (H⁺) to the NH. The HCl is an acid because it donates a proton and the NHis a basebecause it accepts the proton.
